questions.question: A team has stable cycle time, reviewed pull requests, and a clean board. Mid-build, a blocked engineer picks an interpretation of an unanswered product question and ships it. What does this reveal?
options: A work-flow problem; the ticket should have been better specified
An engineering discipline problem; the engineer should have waited
A missing decision flow; open questions have no owner, date, or visible state, so they are answered by whoever is blocked
A prioritization problem; the question should have been resolved before the quarter started
questions.explanation: Boards track work items, and an open decision is not a work item, so it becomes visible only after it has been answered by default. Option A is the answer a competent PM gives, and it is the wrong layer: better tickets reduce the number of open questions but do not create a path for the ones that remain. Option B blames a person for a system with no channel.

questions.question: A team adds a weekly decision review meeting. Which condition determines whether this creates a decision flow?
options: Whether the right people attend consistently
Whether each open question has a latency and a default that fires when the latency is exceeded
Whether decisions are recorded in writing after the meeting
Whether the meeting is held before the sprint planning session
questions.explanation: A ceremony is one way to implement an interface; it is not the interface. Without a latency and an automatic default, a weekly meeting is a place where decisions may or may not happen. Option C is the tempting one because written records are genuinely valuable, and a team that records decisions well can still leave a blocked engineer waiting with no bound and no fallback.

questions.question: A PM maps a delivery system and names herself as owner of the decision flow, the work flow, and the learning flow. What is the strongest objection?
options: Product should not own the learning flow; data should
Three owners is too few; each flow needs a dedicated person
The integration flow is missing from her map
Naming one person for three flows is the same as leaving them unowned when that person is the bottleneck for all three
questions.explanation: The purpose of naming an owner is to give a request a bounded path. If every path leads to the same person, the latency of all three is that person's availability, and nothing has been designed. Option B is the trap for a reader who has learned the four-flow model as a staffing rule: a small team legitimately collapses flows, but it must then say so and accept a shared list, not pretend there are three owners.

questions.question: A team designs a learning flow with a named owner and a monthly readout. Nobody on the team can define the measure, and the instrumentation does not exist. What has been created?
options: A working learning flow; the measure can be defined at the first readout
A meeting, because the gap is a capability gap and ownership does not close it
An interface, because it has an owner and a latency
A decision flow, because the readout will generate decisions
questions.explanation: A named owner produces an answer only if someone can produce the answer. Where the measure and the instrumentation are absent, the readout becomes a discussion. Option A is the optimistic version most teams actually take, and it postpones the capability problem to the moment when a decision depends on it.

questions.question: Noted's team has strong delivery discipline and a thin evidence system. Which pair of flows is most likely to be weak, and why?
options: Decision flow and learning flow, because they fail quietly while delivery metrics stay healthy
Work flow and integration flow, because discipline creates rigidity
Integration flow and learning flow, because both depend on tooling
Decision flow and work flow, because both depend on the PM
questions.explanation: Work and integration flows break loudly, so disciplined teams fix them. Decision and learning flows break silently, and their absence is compatible with excellent cycle time. Option C is plausible on the surface because both do involve tooling, but a team with strong delivery discipline almost always has a working integration flow; that is the flow discipline is usually measured by.
